transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: Fireflies
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Samira (Redwood SE), Aisha (Veridian CTO), Marco (Veridian ML), Priya (Veridian Infra), Jonas (Veridian SWE)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
- Goal: scope POC for inference capacity (reserved GPUs) with burst pool and fallback policies.
- Discussed sizing methodology, benchmark plan, success criteria (latency percentiles, cost per 1M tokens, reliability), timeline and next steps.
- Action items captured to circulate SOW, bench harness and security docs.

Topics: capacity sizing, reserved vs burst, fallback to smaller model/region, bench design, KV cache implications, preemptible instances, SLOs (p95/p99), cost buckets.

[00:00] Lena (Redwood): okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Aisha (Veridian): hi this is Aisha, CTO at Veridian.
[00:15] Marco (Veridian): Marco here, ML lead.
[00:18] Priya (Veridian): Priya, infra.
[00:20] Jonas (Veridian): Jonas, SWE.
[00:22] Daniel (Redwood): Daniel from Redwood, SE. Samira also on the call, she's on mute.

[00:45] Lena: cool, objective today is to agree on success criteria for the POC and nail down how many reserved GPUs you need and what the burst/fallback policies look like, uh and timeline. We have some templates, but we'll tailor them.

[01:12] Marco: quick context — we're building a live recommendation service, multi-tenant, about 200 requests/sec at peak right now, but those are short prompts, avg 80 tokens. We want to evaluate both the 8k and 32k context model variants, because some product paths will require longer context.

[01:45] Daniel: great, are those currently served on cloud GPUs or an in-house cluster?
[01:49] Marco: hybrid — dev on GCP, some prod on private bare-metal. For POC we'd prefer Redwood hosted but with VPC peering so data doesn't leave their environment, that's the ideal.

[02:10] Priya: security caveat — we need SAML SSO and KMS integration for keys, also detailed audit logs.

[02:25] Samira (Redwood): we have a private offering and can do VPC peering and customer-managed KMS. We'll share SOC2 artifacts.

[02:40] Lena: great. So thinking about capacity: typical approach for POC is reserve a baseline pool to hit your p95 latency SLO and then a smaller burst pool to handle spikes. We'll walk through the math — Daniel?

[03:00] Daniel: yeah, quick sketch — step 1: measure single-request latency distribution on candidate model variants at target sequence lengths. Step 2: determine tokens/sec per GPU for your request mix (taking into account KV cache hit rate from repeated prefixes). Step 3: decide baseline throughput needed for target p95 under expected load. Then reserve enough GPUs to cover baseline plus a safety buffer. Burst pool can be either pre-reserved or spot/preemptible instances that we spin up when utilization > threshold. Fallback rules: when burst not available, route to smaller model or lower-precision quantized variant.

[03:55] Marco: can you give a concrete example? numbers would help.

[04:00] Daniel: sure. Example: say the 32k-flavored model averages 12 tokens/ms on an A100-equivalent, with KV cache 40% hit -> effective tokens per second rises because prefix caching reduces decode work. If your average request is 80 input + 40 output tokens, that's 120 tokens per request. So one GPU handles ~ (12 tokens/ms * 1000 ms = 12k tokens/sec) -> ~100 requests/sec. But that's optimistic; p95 can be 2-3x p50 depending on distribution; so for p95 we might model 35-40 requests/sec per GPU. That means 200 rps peak -> baseline 6 GPUs to meet p95, plus 1-2 GPUs buffer.

[05:10] Aisha: that gap between 100 rps and 35 rps — is that the variance from prompts lengths?

[05:18] Daniel: yes. Also batching inefficiencies and cache miss ratios. For small prompts batching helps throughput but hurts latency.

[05:40] Priya: what's your suggestion for burst — preemptible vs fully reserved? We are cost sensitive.

[05:48] Daniel: a common pattern: reserve 60-80% of expected steady-state capacity (SLA-sensitive), then attach a burst pool of preemptible instances (or a smaller GPU family) to absorb spikes. Preemptible is cheaper but risk of preemption; fallback policy must be defined — e.g., degrade to 4-bit quantized model variant or route lower-priority tenants to batch queue.

[06:30] Jonas: how fast can the burst pool spin up? We can't tolerate 30s cold starts for certain flows.

[06:35] Samira: cold-starts depend on image provisioning and model loading — we recommend keeping a warm pool of minimal-sized instances with models loaded in memory (idle but ready) to get <2s warm handoff. For very latency-sensitive endpoints, prefer dedicated reserved pods.

[07:05] Marco: what about KV cache warm-up? If warm pool has KV empty, first long conversation will be slow.

[07:12] Daniel: correct — prefix/KV cache warm-up matters. For chat-style flows you can seed the cache or rely on sticky sessions to keep the same pod. For recommendation stateless calls, caching less useful. We'll simulate cache hit rates in the bench.

[07:45] Lena: success criteria — let's put numbers: 1) p95 latency under 300ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens) for 95% of requests during a 15-minute sustained window; 2) cost per 1M output tokens under $X (placeholder until we exchange pricing); 3) failover mechanism demonstrably reroutes to fallback model with <1% error increase. Thoughts?

[08:30] Aisha: p95 300ms is aggressive for 32k context — maybe we define separate SLOs for short vs long contexts.

[08:40] Lena: agreed. We'll have SLO1 for short context p95 300ms, SLO2 for long context p95 1.2s.

[09:05] Marco: how do you measure cost? do you model tokenization differences and GPU utilization?

[09:12] Daniel: yes, bench will report tokens in/out, GPU utilization by kernel, and estimate $/1M tokens using reserved rate + burst on-demand rate. We'll include a sensitivity analysis for different cache hit rates and burst preemption.

[09:40] Priya: network egress and inter-region routing can add latency — if we host in your region, do you do regional routing?

[09:47] Samira: yes, smart routing by region is supported. We'll pin the POC to a single region you choose to remove cross-region jitter.

[10:10] Daniel: another fallback option is auto-scaling down to a smaller model class in the same family — same tokenizer, shorter context — that keeps semantic parity but reduces tokens/sec load. That is a graceful degrade.

[10:40] Jonas: concerned about correctness regressions when switching models mid-flight. How do we detect quality regressions?

[10:48] Lena: we recommend a small canary prompt set (20-50 prompts) and an automatic similarity/regression check. During fallback we measure score drop and have a policy: if drop > X% escalate to human or block fallback. We'll include the eval harness in the bench.

[11:20] Marco: bench plan — can we run off our representative 1k prompt file?

[11:25] Daniel: yes please. Marco, if you can provide token length distribution and 1k prompt samples that will help us size GPUs accurately. Also indicate which flows must be latency-critical vs background.

[11:45] Marco: will do.

[12:00] Priya: about preemptible instances — in our environment they can be reclaimed fast. Do you support multi-tier burst to fallback to CPU for non-latency flows?

[12:10] Samira: yes, non-latency batch work can be routed to CPU-based quantized runtime; Redwood supports heterogeneous worker pools.

[12:30] Aisha: timeline — how long for POC end-to-end?

[12:35] Lena: typical POC is 3-4 weeks: week 0 onboarding + infra (VPC peering, creds), week 1 baseline bench (single-GPU tests), week 2 scale bench + burst tests, week 3 polish + final report. If you want shorter, compress to 2 weeks with parallel infra work.

[13:05] Marco: our stakeholders want quick wins in 2 weeks. Can we get an initial perf run in first 10 days?

[13:12] Lena: yes — we'll aim for an initial run by day 10. We'll need sample prompts by day 3 and VPC peering by day 6.

[13:40] Daniel: details on metrics we'll collect in bench: p50/p90/p95/p99, cold vs warm latency, GPU utilization, tokens/sec, batch sizes, cache hit rates, and cost breakdown per token by component. We'll also capture abort rates and model fallback events.

[14:10] Priya: do you support tracing to our internal observability? we want spans tagged with request ids.

[14:18] Samira: yes we can push traces to your collector via OTLP; we can also export JSON traces post-run.

[14:35] Lena: security — we'll attach the security pack after the call. It's on the link I'll share in next steps. Anything else?

[14:50] Marco: what about burst sizing rule? how do we pick threshold?

[14:56] Daniel: typical thresholds: spin burst when baseline GPU utilization > 70% for sustained 30s; have cooldown of 60-120s to avoid thrash. For preemptible, maintain at least 1 warm small instance to reduce tail latency. Also set cap on burst cost (e.g., don't exceed X% of baseline cost) and auto-fallback to model degrade if cost cap hits.

[15:40] Aisha: can you document the fallback policy examples? we prefer deterministic rules rather than fuzzy heuristics.

[15:46] Lena: yes we'll propose deterministic policies: e.g., (1) Util > 80% sustained 30s -> open burst pool; (2) if burst unavailable for 45s -> route 10% lowest-priority tenants to quantized variant; (3) if p99 error rises >5% or canary score drop > 7% -> rollback to previous model and alert.

[16:30] Jonas: question on model variants — do you support automatic quantization to 4-bit on the fly?

[16:35] Daniel: runtime supports pre-built quantized variants; real-time quantization is risky. We'll recommend generating and validating quantized variants ahead of POC.

[16:55] Marco: what's the overhead of maintaining multiple model variants? memory, deployment complexity?

[17:00] Samira: memory overhead yes — you need separate model artifacts loaded, but you can co-locate them on instance types with larger memory and small CPU overhead. We'll show a recommended artifact layout.

[17:30] Lena: ok let's capture concrete deliverables — SOW draft + price bands, bench harness + script, security pack, and a schedule for runs. We'll include canary prompts and an eval sheet.

[17:55] Aisha: when you say price bands, do you mean reserved monthly vs on-demand vs burst?

[18:02] Lena: exactly — we'll give you three estimates: reserved monthly commitment, burst spot pricing projection, and blended cost for expected profile.

[18:20] Marco: for the bench run, can we test two scenarios: (A) 200 rps short prompts, (B) 40 rps long-context conversations — to emulate both loads.

[18:30] Daniel: yes, scenario A and B are standard. We'll also run a mixed-traffic run to see behavior.

[18:45] Priya: about logs retention — we need 90-day access for audit.

[18:50] Samira: supported as an add-on. We'll include retention options in SOW.

[19:10] Marco: one more ask — can we throttle certain tenants in real time based on budget?

[19:16] Daniel: yes, Redwood supports per-tenant quotas and rate limits and can tag requests for priority routing.

[19:35] Lena: wrapping up — next steps and owners we'll send after call. Any final risks?

[19:45] Aisha: risk: preemption during peak could cause user-visible errors — need strict fallback tested.

[19:52] Lena: agreed, we'll include preemption drills in bench.

[20:05] Marco: ok thanks everyone, that was helpful.

[20:10] Lena: thanks — we'll send SOW and bench plan by tomorrow.

[20:20] Jonas: thanks, bye.
[20:25] Meeting ends.
